title: B-Trees: Structure, Traversal, Splits, and Balanced Search
description: B-Trees: Structure, Traversal, Splits, and Balanced Search. Interview-first coverage of mechanisms, prediction, diagnosis, and trade-offs.
learningObjectives: Trace a lookup from root to leaf and explain why height matters.
Describe page splits and their maintenance effects.
Separate index navigation from end-to-end query latency.
Trace a B-tree lookup from root to leaf and explain cache hits, storage reads, heap fetches, and latency variability.
Explain b-trees: structure, traversal, splits, and balanced search using the six-layer interview framework.

mentalModel.text: A B-tree is a sorted map built from pages. Each page points you toward a range of keys, like choosing a branch on a road sign. The tree stays balanced, so finding a key takes a small number of page visits even as the table grows. Adding data can split a full page, but it does not normally rebuild the whole index.

blocks.text: A B-tree keeps keys in order and keeps leaf pages at the same depth, so a lookup does not turn into a long chain as the index grows.

A B-tree keeps keys sorted inside pages. Separator keys tell the database which child page could contain a target value. All leaf pages stay at the same depth, so the search path remains balanced as the index grows. The number of child pages each page can point to is called fan-out; higher fan-out usually means fewer levels to traverse.

blocks.title: Why B-trees stay efficient
rows: Many keys per page
Each page can hold many keys and child-page pointers.
The tree needs only a few levels, even for a large table.
Balanced height
Leaf pages stay the same number of steps from the root.
Lookups do not become a long chain as the table grows.
Sorted keys
Keys are kept in order within the tree.
The database can find exact values and scan ranges in order.

blocks.problem: An index contains keys from 1 to 1,000,000. You need key 725,000.
reasoning: Compare the target with separator keys at the root and choose the child range that could contain it.
Repeat at each internal page until reaching a leaf page.
Search the leaf for the key. Many keys fit in each page, so the tree usually has only a few levels.
blocks.outcome: The tree skips unrelated key ranges at each level instead of checking every indexed key.

blocks.text: A lookup follows one path through the tree: root, internal pages, then a leaf.

To find a key, start at the root page, compare the key with the separators, and follow the child range that could contain it. Repeat until you reach a leaf page. If the key is missing, the search still ends at the leaf where it would belong.

blocks.problem: Find key 25 in a B-tree whose root separators are 20 and 40.
reasoning: The root separates keys into ranges: below 20, from 20 up to 40, and 40 or above.
Because 25 is between 20 and 40, follow the middle child page; do not inspect the other ranges.
At the leaf page, look for 25. If it is absent, reaching that leaf tells the database the key is not in the index.
blocks.outcome: A lookup follows one relevant path from root to leaf. The separator values make it possible to skip entire ranges of keys.

blocks.text: Fan-out is the number of child pages an internal page can point to. Higher fan-out usually means fewer levels to traverse.

Databases read and write pages, not one index entry at a time from disk. An internal page can hold many separators, so one page can point to many child pages. Very wide keys fit fewer entries per page and can make the index larger.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: SELECT indexrelname, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS size FROM pg_stat_user_indexes;

blocks.problem: One internal page can point to 200 child pages, and each of those can point to 200 more.
reasoning: The root can cover 200 ranges.
A second level can cover roughly 200 × 200 ranges before reaching the leaves.
Actual capacity depends on page size, key width, page overhead, and how full the pages are.
blocks.outcome: Indexes stay shallow because pages hold many keys and pointers; wider keys can reduce fan-out and increase tree height.

blocks.text: When an index page fills up, PostgreSQL splits it so new entries can fit while searches still follow the correct ranges.

When a page runs out of room, the database splits it and updates the parent so searches still find the right range. If the parent is full too, it can split as well. A root split can add a level to the tree; it is not the same as rebuilding the whole index.

blocks.prompt: Does the existence of an index guarantee PostgreSQL will use it?
blocks.explanation: The planner compares estimated costs, and another access path may be cheaper.

blocks.problem: A full page needs to accept a new key that belongs between its existing keys.
reasoning: The page is split into two pages with entries divided by key order.
The parent is updated with a separator so future searches choose the correct page.
If the parent is also full, the split can propagate upward; a root split adds another level.
blocks.outcome: Splits preserve search correctness, but add write work and can affect page locality.

blocks.text: A split is not a sign that the index is broken. It is how the index makes room while preserving key order. The cost is extra page writes and parent updates; repeated splits can also leave pages less ideally packed or affect locality. The database still maintains the ordering needed for correct lookups.
B-tree lookup depth grows roughly with the logarithm of the number of keys, but query latency is not just a complexity formula.

A balanced B-tree usually finds a key in about log₂(n) levels rather than checking all n keys. Real query time also depends on whether pages are in memory, how many rows match, and how much table data must be fetched.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM users WHERE user_id = 42;

blocks.problem: A lookup touches four index pages and then fetches one table page.
reasoning: If the pages are cached, those visits may be cheap.
If they require storage reads, latency depends on the number and pattern of page reads.
If the query matches thousands of rows, fetching those rows can dominate the initial tree traversal.
blocks.outcome: Big-O explains growth, while the execution plan and buffer behavior explain real performance.

concepts.title: What happens during a real index lookup?

blocks.text: An index lookup is a sequence of page accesses. A page is a fixed-size block of database storage; PostgreSQL commonly uses 8 KB pages by default, though builds can use a different block size. The B-tree stores many keys and child pointers in each page, so a lookup usually visits only a few index pages.

steps.title: Start at the root page
steps.description: PostgreSQL examines separator keys to choose the child range that can contain the email.

steps.title: Follow internal pages
steps.description: At each level, it chooses one child page. It does not scan every key in the index.

steps.title: Find the key in a leaf page
steps.description: The leaf page contains the matching key and the row-location information for the table row.

steps.title: Fetch the table row if needed
steps.description: For a normal index scan, PostgreSQL uses the row location to visit the heap page and read the requested columns. If the needed values are available in the index and visibility checks permit it, an index-only scan may avoid that heap visit.

blocks.text: Each page may already be cached in PostgreSQL's shared buffers or the operating system's page cache. A cache hit avoids a storage read, though PostgreSQL still has CPU and execution work to do. A cache miss may require a random read from the storage device. The table row may be on a different page from the index leaf, so finding the key does not always mean the query has finished.

rows: CPU and memory work on already-cached pages
Nanoseconds to microseconds for individual operations; a database lookup usually involves many operations
No storage wait, but query execution and coordination still take time.
Random read from a fast SSD
Often tens to hundreds of microseconds per read, but can be higher
A cold page access can cost much more than examining a cached page.
Random read from a hard disk
Often several milliseconds
Mechanical seek and rotational delay can dominate a small lookup.
End-to-end database query
Can be sub-millisecond to many milliseconds or more
Depends on page cache, row count, locks, CPU, network, concurrency, and application work.

blocks.title: Do not promise a fixed index latency
blocks.content: These are rough scale examples, not guarantees. An index lookup is not automatically a microsecond query: a cache miss, many matching rows, lock waits, or network round trips can dominate. Measure the actual workload.

blocks.source:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, email, display_name
FROM users
WHERE email = 'aman@example.com';

blocks.problem: The index lookup finds one email, but the endpoint still takes 25 ms.
reasoning: The B-tree traversal may be quick, while the matching heap page is not cached and must be read from storage.
The query may also wait for a connection or lock, or spend time in application and network layers.

Inspect the actual plan and buffer counts. A `shared hit` indicates a page found in PostgreSQL's buffer cache; a `shared read` indicates it had to be read into that cache, though the operating system may have served it from its own cache.
blocks.outcome: An index reduces the search work; it does not eliminate row fetching or other sources of latency. Use `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and application timing to find where the time goes.

blocks.answer: Separators partition the key space; 42 belongs in the middle range.

revisionSheet.text: Search follows ordered separator keys to a relevant leaf.
High fan-out and page layout keep trees shallow.
Splits may propagate upward and a root split can increase height.
O(log n) describes navigation, not necessarily SQL latency.
Heap fetches, visibility, cache state, and result size matter.

questions.prompt: A root has separators 20 and 60. Where should key 42 go?

options.text: The child range between 20 and 60
The range below 20
The range above 60
Every child must be scanned

questions.explanation: Separators partition the key space; 42 belongs in the middle range.

questions.prompt: A B-tree index grows from 3 to 4 levels after many inserts. Which explanation is most consistent with B-tree behavior?

options.text: A root split may have added a level after splits propagated upward.
Every insert adds one level to the tree.
The database has converted the index into a linked list.
The index is necessarily corrupt because balanced trees cannot change height.

questions.explanation: Leaf and parent splits can propagate upward. A root split can increase height, but ordinary inserts do not add a level each time.

questions.prompt: What is the normal search path for a missing key?

options.text: Follow separators to the leaf where the key would be
Scan every leaf
Scan the table because absence cannot be indexed
Rebuild the tree

questions.prompt: A leaf page fills during insertion. What may happen?

options.text: The page splits and parent routing is updated
The whole index must always be rebuilt
Half the entries are discarded
The index turns into a hash table

questions.explanation: Splits create space and update routing; they may cascade.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest complexity explanation?

options.text: O(log n) navigation plus matching-entry and possible heap-fetch costs
Always O(1) because root is cached
Always O(n) because every page is read
The whole query is O(log n) regardless of returned rows

questions.explanation: Total cost depends on matches, heap access, visibility, cache, and I/O.

questions.prompt: Why store many keys per page?

options.text: Page-based storage amortizes reads across many keys
SQL requires one row per page
Pages guarantee no disk I/O
Pages remove the need for ordering

questions.explanation: Page-based storage and fan-out make navigation efficient.

questions.prompt: A primary-key lookup returns one row but takes 180 ms in production. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows one index entry found and several heap blocks read from disk. What is the best next step?

options.text: Investigate heap-page I/O, cache state, and production latency before changing the B-tree.
Replace the B-tree with a hash index because all equality lookups should use hashes.
Add every selected column to the index without checking write or storage cost.
Force index scans globally because the current lookup already uses an index.

questions.explanation: The index can locate the key efficiently while heap I/O dominates latency. Confirm representative buffer and I/O behavior before choosing a covering index or other change.

questions.prompt: A query returns 45% of a large table using a range predicate. The B-tree can produce rows in order, but the plan's index path performs many scattered heap reads. Why might a sequential scan still win?

options.text: Reading a large fraction of the table sequentially may cost less than many scattered heap reads.
B-trees cannot support range predicates.
An index scan is only valid when the predicate matches one row.
A sequential scan always ignores the WHERE clause.

questions.explanation: An index provides an access path, not a guarantee of lower total cost. Selectivity, heap-page locality, ordering, and cache state affect the choice.

questions.prompt: Which can increase B-tree maintenance or footprint?

options.text: Wide keys reduce entries per page.
Splits may require page and parent updates.
Every lookup scans all keys.
Updates to indexed values require maintenance.

questions.explanation: Wide keys, splits, and indexed-column changes add cost; normal lookups do not scan all keys.

questions.prompt: Which can dominate latency after index entries are found?

options.text: Random heap page fetches
Visibility checks and filtering
Returning many rows
The logarithmic notation itself

questions.explanation: Index navigation is only one part of execution.

questions.prompt: Balanced B-tree leaves remain at the same depth.
questions.explanation: Balanced depth bounds the search path.

questions.prompt: If a B-tree exists, PostgreSQL must use it.
questions.explanation: The planner compares costs and may prefer a sequential scan.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A unique-key lookup is fast in a microbenchmark but slow under production load. Diagnose causes and evidence.
strongAnswerPoints: Compare cache behavior, actual rows, concurrency, and storage latency.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: The tree bounds the search path, but heap reads, visibility checks, cache misses, and contention can dominate. Capture the real plan and buffers, compare estimates to actual rows, and measure representative concurrency before changing the index.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A write-heavy table has insert latency spikes. How could B-tree behavior contribute, and what would you measure?
strongAnswerPoints: Every relevant index adds write work.
Splits may add page writes and routing updates.
Measure WAL, I/O, index size, and write latency.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: Inserts maintain relevant indexes and splits may add writes. Validate with workload metrics, inventory redundant indexes, and test any design change against both read and write workloads.
